skill.name: Take account of the other side
skill.why: Answering the other side makes an argument much harder to knock down.
skill.how: Look for both halves: what the other side thinks, then the writer's answer.

steps.say: My fish-finger custard is the best! But not everyone agrees with me.

show.text: Fish-finger custard is the best dessert.
show.nudge: That's Mo's own side. Who disagrees?

show.text: Some people say it's too lumpy.

show.nudge: That just says when Mo makes it. Who disagrees?

steps.ask: Tap what people who disagree with Mo think.
steps.win: Yes! That's the other side's view. Writers call it the counter-argument.

steps.say: Now I answer it with a reason.

show.text: but the lumps are real banana.

steps.ask: What does 'the lumps are real banana' do?

options.text: names another worry
options.reason: Nobody is worrying in this half. It's Mo talking back.

agrees the custard is bad

steps.win: Yes! That answer is the rebuttal. Both halves together take account of the other side.

steps.say: Careful! Zed's sign names the worry, then stops.

steps.win: Right! Only half doesn't count. A counter-argument needs a rebuttal.

steps.ask: Tap the one that names the other side and answers it.

steps.say: The answer has to fit the worry. Lumpy? Then talk about the lumps!

encounters.text: To the School Council. Our sports day is held every year in the second week of February, often the hottest week on Bluster Rock. Last year, it reached forty-one degrees, and three students were taken to the first aid tent before lunch. The tug-of-war rope was so hot that nobody wanted to touch it. We think sports day should move to May, when the mornings are cool and the oval is still dry. Some argue that May is when lots of families go camping up the coast, but May mornings are much cooler. encounters.frame: An opinion piece in the Bluster Rock Bugle is about a new marine sanctuary. Wren has circled it twice.
encounters.text: SAVE CORAL GULLY, by marine scientist Dr Lena Moss. Coral Gully, on the northern side of Bluster Rock, is home to the island's last healthy patch of reef. In the past five years, our surveys have found that the number of fish on the reef has fallen by almost half. I believe the council should make Coral Gully a no-fishing sanctuary, where the reef can rest and recover. I know that many fishing families fear the sanctuary will leave their nets empty. Some say a sanctuary will hurt fishing, but the reef deserves a rest after fifty years of nets. Healthy reefs also attract snorkellers, who spend about $2 million a year in local cafes, dive shops and caravan parks. At Pelican Point, catches just outside a sanctuary doubled within ten years of it opening. That happens because fish grow large and breed inside the protected area, then spill out into the water around it. Coral Gully has the island's last 300 giant clams, which have nearly vanished elsewhere. The council will decide at its meeting on the first Monday of next month. I urge every resident who cares about the reef to come along and speak up. Copies of our survey results are available at the library.
encounters.prompt: Dr Moss names the fishing families' fear of empty nets. Which sentence would do most to change their minds?
encounters.success: The worry is empty nets. Pelican Point shows catches grew next to a sanctuary. That fits the worry best.

encounters.frame: The council wants to pull down the Big Galah, Bluster Rock's giant pink statue. Indi has written a speech to save it.
encounters.prompt: Councillor Fitz says the Big Galah costs too much to keep. Tap the sentence that answers him best.
encounters.success: The worry is cost. A coat of paint is far cheaper than knocking it down. That answer fits.

parts: Councillors, for forty years the Big Galah has stood beside the highway, welcoming every traveller to Bluster Rock with its enormous pink crest. Families pull over to take photos beneath it. When the highway was widened twenty years ago, the whole town signed a petition to keep it, and the road was moved around its feet instead. Even the Countaby salutes it every morning.

parts.tap: Some say it costs too much, but the Big Galah is loved by everyone in town.
parts.reason: It has 'some say' and 'but', yet being loved isn't about cost. It misses the worry.

parts.tap: Last summer alone, more than six thousand visitors signed the guestbook at its feet.
parts.reason: This shows the Galah is popular. It doesn't show it's cheap to keep.

parts.tap: The cafe next door sells more galah-shaped biscuits than any other item on its menu.
parts.reason: That's money for the cafe, not the council. It doesn't make the Galah cheaper to keep.

parts.tap: Tearing it down would cost more than eight thousand dollars, while a fresh coat of pink would cost less than four hundred.
Anyone who wants to knock down a giant galah clearly has no sense of fun.
parts.reason: This insults people instead of answering their worry with a reason.

parts: The Big Galah has watched over this town for longer than most of us have been alive. I am asking you, tonight, to let it keep watching.

encounters.prompt: Critics fear a robot could break down while someone is in trouble. Put each reply in the right box.

items.text: Admittedly, robots can break down, but they don't need lunch breaks.

items.text: Every robot runs a self-check each morning and stays off the beach if anything is faulty.

items.text: Every robot comes with a five-year factory warranty that pays for repairs.

items.text: Robots can break, but each one works beside a human lifeguard who can take over in seconds.

items.text: Some say robots break down, but robots are clearly the future of our beaches.

items.text: Each robot carries two batteries, so it keeps running if one of them fails.

items.text: Critics also forget how cheap the robots are to run each summer.

encounters.frame: The council might ban busking in the Bluster Rock mall. Zed summed up a busker's speech, but got one part wrong.
encounters.text: Speech by Rosa Delgado, street musician. I have played my guitar outside the Bluster Rock bakery every Saturday morning for six years. In that time, I've played for tourists, toddlers, grumpy truck drivers and one very confused emu. I want to talk about the plan to ban busking in the mall. Some shop owners find the music distracting, and a few say it makes it hard to talk to customers. I hear them. A simple rule that buskers must move every hour and keep the volume low would fix that problem, without silencing anyone. Music also brings people into the mall, and people who stop to listen often stay to buy a coffee or a pie. The bakery owner, Mr Lam, told me his Saturday sales are the best of the week. Other towns have banned buskers, and some say their main streets became quiet and empty. Please don't make that mistake here. Let the music stay, and let's write some fair rules together. Rosa finished by playing a short song she had written about the mall, and three councillors tapped their feet. One of them even hummed along on the way out.

encounters.success: The worry is distraction. Moving every hour and playing softly fixes exactly that, with no 'but' needed.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote two drafts of a paragraph for the Reef Rays newsletter. She wants the one that deals with the other side best.
encounters.text:
Tully's note: The newsletter goes to every family in the club, including the fans who love the old Saturday games. I want those fans to feel listened to, not told off. So I wrote two drafts, and the Countaby has already chewed the corner of one.

DRAFT A: In my view, the girls' footy teams deserve the same Saturday time slot as the boys' teams at the Bluster Rock oval. Girls' footy is growing fast, and last season our under-12s won the cup. Some fans say the boys have always played on Saturdays, but our girls' teams are really good this year. The club should share the Saturday slot fairly from next season.

DRAFT B: In my view, the girls' footy teams deserve the same Saturday time slot as the boys' teams at the Bluster Rock oval. Girls' footy is growing fast, and last season our under-12s won the cup. The boys have played on Saturdays for more than fifty years, and many fans are used to it. Yet tradition alone is no reason to keep the girls on a weeknight, when half their families can't come to watch. The club should share the Saturday slot fairly from next season.
encounters.prompt: Which draft takes better account of the other side, and why?
encounters.success: Draft B answers the tradition point head on: tradition alone isn't a reason. Draft A's 'but' talks about something else.

options.text: Draft A, because 'some fans say' and 'but' show both sides.
options.reason: Draft A names the fans' view, but 'really good this year' doesn't answer the point about tradition.

options.text: Draft B, because it is longer and gives more facts.
options.reason: Length isn't the test. Does the answer fit the fans' point about tradition?

options.text: Draft B, because its answer deals with the tradition point itself.
Draft A, because it's shorter, so fans will read to the end.
options.reason: Short is fine, but Draft A's answer misses the fans' point about tradition.

encounters.frame: The Countaby found an article about the ghost tours at the old Bluster Rock cemetery.
encounters.text:
KEEP THE LANTERN TOURS, by Ezra Finch, tour guide. For twelve years, the Lantern Tours have led visitors through the old Bluster Rock cemetery after dark, telling the true stories of the miners, cooks and camel drivers who built this town. Each tour raises money to repair the crumbling headstones, and last year we fixed thirty-one of them. Visitors come from all over the country, and many are descendants of the people buried there, hoping to learn more about their own families. Without the tours, these stories would be forgotten, and the headstones would keep falling apart.

Some neighbours have complained that the tours are noisy, and that torch beams shine through their bedroom windows late at night. They are right, and I am sorry. From next month, every tour will finish by half past eight, and our guides will use red lanterns, which are far dimmer than torches. We will also stay on the paths at the far end, well away from the houses.

The Lantern Tours bring history to life in a way no textbook can. Last month, a Year 5 class joined a tour and wrote a whole book about the camel drivers. Our guides are all volunteers, and they would be heartbroken to stop. I hope the council will let them continue.
encounters.prompt: In the second paragraph, why does Ezra say the neighbours are right before giving his new rules?
encounters.success: Admitting they're right shows Ezra listened. Then his fix answers their worry, so they're more likely to agree.

options.text: He has changed his mind, and now he wants the council to stop the Lantern Tours for good.
options.reason: He still asks for the tours to continue in the last paragraph.

options.text: He wants the council to think the neighbours' complaints are unfair.
options.reason: He says the neighbours are right. That's the opposite of calling them unfair.

options.text: Agreeing first shows he has listened, so the neighbours are more likely to accept his fix.
He needs more evidence that the tours raise money for the headstones.
options.reason: The headstone money is in the first paragraph. The second is all about the neighbours.
